Conversant
kŏn´vẽr-sănt
adj. (dwelling among; having habitual intercourse with — rendering Hebrew halak, to walk)
Latin conversari, to turn oneself about among, to keep company with. The older English kept the sense of living among; the modern sense of being well informed is a late thinning of the word.

Biblical Definition

Conversant in the Authorized Version means dwelling among, keeping daily company with, and it stands behind the older English word conversation, which meant a manner of life and not talk. Joshua reads the law before the whole congregation, “with the women, and the little ones, and the strangers that were conversant among them” (Jos 8:35) — the strangers who lived among Israel, whose lives were bound up with hers. David's men are described by Nabal's servant: “the men were very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields” (1Sa 25:15). The Hebrew is the ordinary verb to walk; being conversant with a man is walking with him, and the test of what a man is comes out in that walking. This is exactly why the New Testament uses conversation for the whole visible life: “Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ” (Php 1:27), and “as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation” (1Pe 1:15). A man's doctrine is heard; his conversation is watched. Nabal's shepherds did not report David's creed; they reported that nothing went missing in the fields.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines conversant as keeping company; having frequent or customary intercourse; living among or with; and secondarily, acquainted by familiar use or study.

expand to see more

CON'VERSANT, a. Keeping company; having frequent or customary intercourse; intimately associating; familiar by fellowship.

2. Acquainted by familiar use or study; as, a man conversant with the Scriptures.

3. Concerning; having concern or relation to; as, education is conversant about the young.

CONVERSA'TION, n. General course of manners; behavior; deportment; especially as it respects morals.

Key Scripture

Joshua 8:35 — "There was not a word of all that Moses commanded, which Joshua read not before all the congregation of Israel, with the women, and the little ones, and the strangers that were conversant among them."

1 Samuel 25:15 — "But the men were very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields:"

Philippians 1:27 — "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;"

1 Peter 1:15 — "But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation;"

Modern Corruption

The word has thinned from a life lived among men to information possessed about a subject, and the same thinning has happened to Christian profession.

expand to see more

To be conversant once meant to dwell with; it now means to be informed about. A man may be perfectly conversant with the doctrine of sanctification in the modern sense and utterly unsanctified in the older one. The drift is not merely lexical. Where Christianity is understood as a body of information to be mastered, church life becomes the transfer of content and the visible walk drops out of the test entirely. Scripture measures otherwise. Nabal's servant vouched for David's men on the evidence of months in the fields: nothing hurt, nothing missing.

Joshua 8:35 carries a second charge worth naming. The whole law was read before the women, the little ones, and the strangers conversant among them — nobody was reckoned incapable of hearing the word of God, and nobody was excused from it. Where a congregation is sorted into audiences and the strangers among it are given something lighter than the Scriptures, that assembly has not become welcoming; it has withheld from its hearers the only thing it was given to hand them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew halak (H1980), to walk, go, live among; the Authorized Version renders it conversant where the walking is a settled dwelling with others. Greek anastrophe (G391), manner of life, lies behind the New Testament conversation.

expand to see more

Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, go, behave; Joshua 8:35 and 1 Samuel 25:15 of dwelling among.

Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conduct; 1 Peter 1:15, Galatians 1:13, Ephesians 4:22.

Greek politeuomai (G4176) — to live as a citizen; Philippians 1:27, where the conversation is to become the gospel.

Latin conversari, to turn about among — the old English kept the dwelling, the modern kept only the knowing.

Wherever the Authorized Version says conversation it means the whole visible life, never speech alone.

Usage

"“The strangers that were conversant among them” — and the whole law was read in their hearing."

"“As long as we were conversant with them” — character proved by months in the fields."

"“Holy in all manner of conversation” — the walk, not the talk."
